 Apple vs Microsoft: iPhone Concentration and Microsoft Cloud Growth
 10 minute read | Apr 1, 2026 | Reviewed by Howie Mann 
 AAPL MSFT Comparison 
 Apple sells consumer hardware and runs a large digital services business across its installed base. It earns money from iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch and AirPods sales, and from Services such as the App Store, advertising, AppleCare, iCloud, licensing and payment services.
 Microsoft sells productivity software, cloud computing, developer tools, operating systems and gaming products to consumers and businesses. It earns money from Microsoft 365 subscriptions, Azure cloud usage, Windows and device licences, LinkedIn, Xbox and Activision gaming, and search advertising.
 Revenue 
 Apple’s trailing-twelve-month revenue of $435.6B is roughly 43% larger than Microsoft’s $305.5B, but the gap is narrowing. Between fiscal years 2022 and 2025, Apple grew revenue at a 1.8% compound annual rate and added about $22B of sales. Microsoft grew at 12.4% over the same window and added roughly $83B.
 The mix behind each top line differs sharply. More than half of Apple’s revenue still comes from a single product line, iPhone, which grew 0.7% compound annual over three years. Microsoft’s revenue is dominated by subscription software and cloud services, where usage and pricing compound to produce double-digit growth.

Every dollar of Services revenue therefore contributes roughly twice the gross profit of a dollar of hardware. That mix shift is the mechanism behind consolidated gross margin rising from 43.3% in FY2022 to 46.9% in FY2025.

 The emergence of AI at the Edge marks a familiar transition in computing history. Just as computing evolved from centralized mainframes to minicomputers, workstations, personal computers, and cloud architectures, AI is now expanding beyond centralized data centres to where data is created and decisions are made.
Apple's recent hardware announcements underscore this shift by emphasizing on-device AI, where inference is performed locally on increasingly capable consumer hardware. This reflects a broader industry trend toward distributing AI compute across billions of endpoint devices, reducing latency, improving privacy, lowering bandwidth requirements, and enabling resilient, offline-capable intelligence.
There is a useful historical parallel. During the 1970s, researchers working on the DEC PDP series developed technologies and ideas that contributed to the creation of UNIX. As UNIX matured, it became increasingly decoupled from proprietary hardware, allowing the operating system and its ecosystem to spread across many platforms. That unbundling accelerated innovation by separating software value from the underlying hardware.
A similar unbundling is underway in AI. Rather than intelligence being tied exclusively to hyperscale cloud infrastructure, AI models, inference engines, accelerators, and application frameworks are becoming portable across cloud, enterprise, and edge environments. Competitive advantage is shifting away from centralized compute alone toward orchestration, governance, interoperability, and the ability to generate measurable value wherever intelligence is deployed.
The next phase of AI will not be defined solely by larger models or larger data centres. It will be defined by the intelligent distribution of compute and inference across an interconnected ecosystem spanning cloud, edge, and endpoint devices.

 In 2014, Microsoft was at real risk of becoming irrelevant.
Mobile had passed them by. The Nokia acquisition had flopped. The cloud was emerging, and plenty of people doubted Microsoft could lead there at all.
Then Satya Nadella stepped in with a direction that unsettled almost everyone. Pivot to cloud-first. Rethink Windows. Open up to competitors. Even put Microsoft software on Apple devices. For a company built on its own walled garden, this was close to a complete reversal.
What happened next is the part I want leaders to notice.
The board did not rubber-stamp it. They wrestled with it. Some directors worried it would alienate loyal enterprise customers. Others feared the company was abandoning its identity. The tension in the room was real.
And it was useful.
Because true consensus does not mean smoothing over disagreement until everyone nods. It means letting the room wrestle until clarity emerges. It is slower. It is messier. But it does something a quick vote never can. It builds ownership.
By the time Microsoft committed to cloud-first, the board was not merely aligned. They were invested, because every director had helped shape the path. So when the early results were uncertain, the strategy held.
The lesson is not just about Microsoft. The best teams do not fear tension. They use it to sharpen thinking and deepen trust.
When everyone has truly been heard, commitment is not forced. It is earned.
